lines: * 🔀 It's also a low priority reference, so a leak trace reaches the value through any other holder it has, and only names the map when the map is the only thing left holding it. An entry waiting to be expunged is rarely what someone wants to be sent to fix.

* 🔨 Object ids are now written in hex wherever Shark writes one for someone to read: leak trace labels, `HeapObject.toString()`, error messages, the Shark CLI and the heap explorer of the LeakCanary activity. `instance @314615480 of com.example.Foo` now reads `instance @0x12c0a6b8 of com.example.Foo`, the way heap dump viewers write an address, so an id copied out of a leak trace can be searched for in one. An object above the 2 GB mark of a 32 bit heap dump is written as its address too, where it used to come out negative. Leak signatures don't change.
* 🔀 In the Shark CLI's interactive mode, the `ID` of `instance CLASS_NAME@ID` and the other commands is read as hex, with or without the `0x`.

-* 🐛 A leak trace could start at a `NATIVE_STACK` or `JNI_LOCAL` GC root, an object that native code running on a thread holds, typically for the length of a call. Shark reads what Java code running on a thread holds, its `JAVA_FRAME` roots, as low priority references from that thread, so that a leak trace goes through any other path to the same object first. It read the native roots of the same thread as GC roots like any other, so a leak trace started there whenever that path was the shortest. In one production heap dump, the JIT compiler thread held the app's `PathClassLoader` while compiling one of its classes, and the leak trace went from that thread's native stack through the class loader to the static field holding the leak, instead of starting at the `Thread.contextClassLoader` that holds the same class loader for good. That leak keeps its fingerprint, since every object in the part of its trace that changed is expected. A thread's native roots are now read the same way as its Java frames, and print as `<Java Local>` in a leak trace too. A native root whose thread isn't in the heap dump is a low priority GC root, as a Java frame is.

* 🔀 A `javaLocal()` reference matcher now matches what native code running on that thread holds as well. So the default matchers ignore the native roots of the main thread, as they already ignored its Java frames, and a leak trace that started at the `MessageQueue` the main thread holds while it waits for its next message now starts at `ActivityThread.sMainThreadHandler`.

+    * ⚠️ `ReferenceLocationType` and `LeakTraceReference.ReferenceType` have a new `NATIVE_LOCAL` constant for those references, so an exhaustive `when` over either needs a branch for it. A Java frame is still `LOCAL`.
### Breaking change: `Leaking: YES` / `NO` is now `Verdict: Stuck` / `Expected`

* ⚠️ `ObjectReporter.leakingReasons` and `notLeakingReasons` are now `stuckReasons` and `expectedReasons`. These are what a custom `ObjectInspector` adds to, so every inspector needs the rename — see [Identifying leaking objects and labeling objects](recipes.md#identifying-leaking-objects-and-labeling-objects).

* 🔀 A verdict that comes from another object on the trace says so in the same words: `Activity↓ is not leaking` is now `Activity↓ is expected`, and `Activity↑ is leaking` is now `Activity↑ is stuck`. The two built in reasons changed with them: `a class is never leaking` is now `a class is always expected`, and `A ClassLoader is never leaking` is now `a ClassLoader is always expected`. An inspector of your own that worded a reason around "leaking" still reads as it always did — these are the strings LeakCanary itself writes.

* 🔀 Heap analyses stored by an earlier version can't be read back. Java serialization writes field names and enum constant names, so a stored analysis would have come back with a null verdict on a property declared non-null; `LeakTraceObject`'s `serialVersionUID` is bumped so that it fails to deserialize instead. LeakCanary's own database drops and recreates its tables, which loses the heap analyses already in it — the heap dumps they were made from are usually long gone, so there was nothing to rewrite them from.

-* 🔀 Android Studio's Profiler has a LeakCanary task that, in its on-device mode, reads LeakCanary's logcat output and parses `Leaking: (YES|NO|UNKNOWN)` out of it. It will report a parsing failure against this version until Studio updates. Its other mode, where Studio analyzes the heap dump itself with its own bundled copy of Shark, is unaffected.

+* 🔀 Android Studio's Profiler has a LeakCanary task that, in its on-device mode, reads LeakCanary's logcat output and parses `Leaking: (YES|NO|UNKNOWN)` out of it. It will report a parsing failure against this version until Studio updates, and the update will need to recognize `<Native Local>` alongside `<Java Local>`. * 🐤 [#3006](https://github.com/square/leakcanary/pull/3006) Automatic fix of the AOSP leak where `InputMethodManager.mImeInsetsConsumer` holds the window of a dialog that was dismissed while its focus gain was still queued, which happens when a dialog is shown then dismissed while the main thread is busy. The fix applies on Android 11 to Android 15: Android 16 doesn't set that field anymore.

* 🐤 [#3008](https://github.com/square/leakcanary/pull/3008) Automatic fix of the AOSP leak where an activity relaunched with its window preserved leaves `DecorContext.mActivityContext` pointing at the destroyed activity. `DecorView.getResources()` reads that weak reference on every call, which keeps the destroyed activity alive through garbage collections while the window draws, so LeakCanary reported it as retained and then found no leak in the heap dump. Android preserves the window when an overlay the app uses changes, e.g. the navigation mode or the accent color, which relaunches every activity, and when an activity is resized in multi-window mode. The fix applies on Android 10: Android 11 fixed the leak.

* 🐛 LeakCanary sometimes dumped the heap for objects that its own garbage collection had just collected, and the analysis of that heap dump then found no leak. Before dumping, LeakCanary runs a GC and counts the watched objects that are still retained, by polling the reference queue their weak references go to once they're cleared. ART clears a weak reference during the GC, but only puts it on its queue afterwards, from its `ReferenceQueueDaemon` thread, so an object collected by the last of the GCs `FinalizingInProcessGcTrigger.runGc()` runs was counted as still retained. The last GC is the one that collects whatever the first one couldn't, such as a destroyed window that is only reachable through a weak reference which something reads while the GC is marking: reading it keeps the window alive through that GC, the same way `ObjectAnimator` keeps the objects it animates alive. `runGc()` now waits for the daemon before returning. That also spares `LeakAssertions.assertNoLeaks()` a heap dump and an analysis in that situation. In the debug builds of a large app, a third of the heap dumps LeakCanary took found no leak, and in 21 of the 24 we looked at, this is what had happened.
